newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China currency rules good for JV - Morgan Stanley.
newsitem.headline: China currency rules good for JV - Morgan Stanley.

text.p: Morgan Stanley's landmark joint venture in China remains a good strategy as long as the yuan is not fully convertible on the capital account, John Wadsworth, chairman of Morgan Stanley Asia, said Wednesday.

"Our strategy envisions that the renminbi becomes convertible in about 2001 or 2002 and that is an important date," Wadsworth told a seminar sponsored by the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong.
"If we felt the convertibility on the capital account was going to come sooner, the CICC strategy would not be a smart one for us," he said.
Morgan Stanley is a 35 percent partner in a joint venture with Construction Bank of China, which holds 42.5 percent of the the firm, China International Capital Corp (CICC).
Chinese, Hong Kong and Singapore firms hold the balance.
CICC, which was set up in August 1995, is China's first joint venture investment bank.

As long as the yuan cannot be converted on the capital account, Morgan Stanley benefits from having a joint venture investment firm within China while its competitors look on from across the country's borders.
"It gives us the opportunity to build a business without competition," Wadsworth said.

While China is expected to grant similar licenses in time, "the government has said very clearly that this is an experiment and they want to see how this works before they grant additional licenses," he said.
Successes of the joint venture include raising foreign capital for state-owned Jilin Oil Group, Wadsworth noted.
Looking forward, the joint venture is looking to develop business in China's foreign exchange and government bond market.
"It is really the development of the Chinese government bond market that is the single most important opportunty for us," Wadsworth said.
He noted that both the foreign exchange and bond markets still are in the early stages of development, but that the China has made important strides in developing these.
But more needs to be done and Morgan Stanley is working with the government to help develop modern markets, Wadsworth said.
He said that it is still too early for Morgan Stanley to get heavily involved in China's A-share market, "though through CICC we will develop ways of getting into the market."
And it is still too early for China to get involved in derivatives, which require efficient cash markets.

Wadsworth forecast a bright future for Shanghai financial markets, but said their internationalization is tied to capital account convertibility. Until then, Hong Kong will remain the financing conduit to China.
Hong Kong's importance to China means that its markets will prosper much more in the remaining years of this century than those of Singapore, Wadsworth predicted.
